question: Mr. Osei has a new intermediate class and wants to teach it well. He gives every student an online questionnaire that sorts them into visual, auditory, and kinesthetic learners, and he plans to prepare three separate versions of each lesson so that each student receives instruction matched to their diagnosed style. A colleague asks whether this is the best use of his planning time. Drawing on what the course teaches about learner differences and about lesson planning, what should Mr. Osei do instead, and why?
answer: Mr. Osei is about to spend his planning time on the one step the evidence does not support. Sorting students by diagnosed style and matching instruction to it is the meshing hypothesis, and Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, and Bjork (2008) found no adequate evidence that it improves outcomes; the failure is the diagnose-and-restrict method, not the reality of learner differences. He should instead plan one whole-class lesson that moves through a variety of activity formats, giving every student more than one route into the material, which is the course's evidence-consistent recommendation and sound lesson planning at the same time.
anchor: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, and Bjork (2008) found no adequate evidence that identifying a learner's preferred style and then matching instruction to that style produces better learning outcomes.
